procedural_history.originating_court: Not specified in the provided text.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 17.12.2012 of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh in CRA No. 1176 DB of 2010 and 1222 DB of 2010.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh issued a Judgment and Order on 17.12.2012 in Criminal Appeal Nos. 1176 DB of 2010 and 1222 DB of 2010.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants (represented by Ahmed Faraz Khan and Deepak Goel) appealed to the Supreme Court against the High Court's Judgment and Order. The case was heard in the Supreme Court as Criminal Appeal Nos. 2301-2302 of 2014.

decision.conviction_status: The conviction of the appellants under Section 302 IPC read with Section 34 IPC is modified as conviction under Section 304 Part-I IPC.
decision.sentence_status: The appellants are sentenced to undergo imprisonment for seven years.
directions: Appellant Gurwinder Singh is ordered to be released forthwith unless his presence is required in any other case.
Appellant Satnam Singh is directed to surrender to serve the remaining period of sentence, failing which, he shall be taken into custody.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellants under Section 302 IPC (murder) should be altered to a conviction under Section 304 Part-I IPC (culpable homicide not amounting to murder) on the grounds that the incident occurred during a scuffle.

facts: The incident occurred when both parties assembled to settle a land dispute.
An exchange of words escalated into a sudden scuffle between the parties, who were initially unarmed.
During the scuffle, one appellant (G) went into a room, brought an axe, and struck the victim on the head while the other appellant (S) held him.
The appellants also sustained injuries in the incident, which the prosecution failed to explain.
The victim, who was found to be drunk, survived for about a month before succumbing to his injuries.
There was a five-day delay in filing the police report (FIR) as settlement talks were still ongoing.
law: The Court applied "Exception 4 to Section 300" of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).

This exception states that an act is considered culpable homicide not amounting to murder if it is committed without premeditation, in a sudden fight, in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, and without the offender having taken undue advantage or acted in a cruel or unusual manner.
application: The Court determined that the incident was not premeditated, as it arose from a "sudden quarrel" and "scuffle" during a meeting to resolve a dispute.
It noted that both parties were initially unarmed, and it was only during the scuffle that the weapon was introduced.
The Court found that the appellants did not take "undue advantage," reasoning that the victim survived for a month after the attack and that the appellants themselves sustained injuries.
The non-explanation of the appellants' injuries was considered a significant factor supporting the conclusion that it was a sudden fight rather than a one-sided, premeditated attack.
Based on these circumstances, the Court concluded that the appellants' act fell under Exception 4, making it culpable homicide rather than murder.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the act fell under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC. However, because the weapon used (an axe) and the nature of the head injuries established an intention to cause an injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, the Court altered the conviction from Section 302 IPC (murder) to the lesser offense of Section 304 Part-I IPC (culpable homicide not amounting to murder) and reduced the sentence to seven years imprisonment.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellants under Section 302 IPC (murder) should be altered to a conviction under Section 304 Part-I IPC (culpable homicide not amounting to murder) on the grounds that the incident occurred during a scuffle.
appellant_arguments: Even if the prosecution's accusations are accepted, the offence does not amount to murder under Section 302 IPC because the attack occurred during a sudden quarrel when the parties had gathered to settle a land dispute.
The prosecution's case is doubtful due to a five-day delay in lodging the First Information Report.
The prosecution suppressed the true origin of the incident and failed to explain the injuries sustained by the accused, suggesting the complainant party were the aggressors.
respondent_arguments: The conviction for murder under Section 302 IPC was justified, considering the evidence adduced by the prosecution and the nature of the head injuries inflicted on the deceased.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: It is not an invariable rule that the complainant party is considered the aggressor merely because the accused sustained injuries in the same transaction, nor is the prosecution under an absolute obligation to explain such injuries.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the prosecution is not invariably obligated to explain injuries sustained by an accused during an incident, nor does the presence of such injuries automatically prove that the complainant party were the aggressors. The burden to explain the accused's injuries only falls upon the prosecution if two specific conditions are met: the injuries occurred during the same transaction and they are of a serious nature.
legal_tests_applied: Before placing the burden on the prosecution to explain the injuries on the person of the accused, two conditions are to be satisfied:- (i) the injuries were sustained by the accused in the same transaction; and (ii) the injuries sustained by the accused are serious in nature.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the prosecution's failure to explain injuries on the accused should lead to the case being disbelieved was rejected. The court clarified that this is not an invariable proposition of law and is subject to a two-part test regarding the timing and seriousness of the injuries.
why_respondent_won: The respondent (prosecution) successfully argued against the proposition that their case should be disbelieved merely for failing to explain the accused's injuries. The court affirmed that there is no absolute rule requiring the prosecution to explain such injuries unless specific conditions are met.
